tasks.purpose: 讨论社区运动设施的使用方式
tasks.setting: Some people believe that local councils should make community sports facilities free for everyone. Others think that users should pay a small fee so that the facilities can be maintained and improved. Both approaches would affect how these public spaces are funded.
tasks.lead: Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
bullets: Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
must: 解释免费使用与收取少量费用两种观点，并以理由和相关例证支持个人判断。
tasks.model:
Community sports facilities can make exercise accessible to a wide range of residents, but they also cost money to maintain. Some people therefore favour free access, while others prefer a modest charge. In my view, councils should keep basic use free and seek other funding for improvements.

The strongest argument for charging users is that a dependable source of income can help protect the facilities themselves. Swimming pools, for example, need cleaning, equipment checks and qualified staff. If a council has to meet all these costs from its general budget, repairs may be postponed whenever other services face pressure. A small admission fee could give managers some money specifically for upkeep, making it less likely that a pool or court becomes unusable.

Nevertheless, even a modest fee can discourage regular use when it is paid by several family members or on repeated visits. Free entry removes that immediate barrier and allows residents to try an activity without committing money they may need elsewhere. A teenager who can visit a local court after school, for instance, may be able to exercise regularly even if organised clubs are beyond the family's budget. The benefit is not confined to the individual: well-used public spaces can also provide opportunities for neighbours to meet.

I accept that free access does not make maintenance free. Councils must still plan for the costs, and they could charge for optional services such as equipment hire or private coaching. However, making ordinary entry depend on payment would place the burden most directly on those whom public provision is intended to include. Protecting access should therefore take priority, provided that a realistic maintenance budget is agreed.

In conclusion, user fees offer a useful contribution to upkeep, but free basic access better serves the community as a whole. Optional charges and planned public funding can help maintain facilities without excluding residents from everyday use.

tasks.purpose: 讨论学校如何安排户外学习
tasks.setting: Some people think that schools should devote regular lesson time to learning outdoors in local parks and gardens. Others believe that this time should be spent in classrooms, where teachers can use equipment and keep lessons more predictable. Both views concern how pupils learn.
tasks.lead: Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
bullets: Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
must: 解释定期户外学习与将课时用于课堂学习两种观点，并以理由和相关例证支持个人判断。
tasks.model:
Schools must decide how best to use limited lesson time. While some people favour regular learning in parks and gardens, others prefer the stability and resources of the classroom. I believe that outdoor lessons deserve a regular place in the timetable, although they should complement rather than replace classroom teaching.

Classrooms offer conditions that make many activities easier to organise. Teachers can prepare materials in advance, display written instructions and ensure that pupils have access to desks and equipment. A science lesson involving careful measurements, for example, may be more practical indoors, where instruments can be protected and results recorded consistently. Classroom routines can also help pupils who need a quiet, predictable environment to concentrate. These advantages make it sensible to retain indoor lessons as the foundation of the school day.

Outdoor learning, however, can give pupils direct access to things that are difficult to understand solely from a description. In a garden, a class studying plants can compare leaves, observe the conditions in which different species grow and return later to look for changes. Such observations give the teacher concrete evidence to discuss when pupils are back inside. A local park can similarly provide a setting for measuring distances or examining how a public space is used.

There are limits: poor weather, travel time and accessibility can make some visits unsuitable. Schools should therefore choose nearby sites and provide alternatives when an outdoor activity would exclude a pupil or disrupt another essential lesson. These practical constraints justify careful planning, but they do not justify abandoning outdoor work altogether. Even a short, well-prepared visit can create material for several subsequent classroom activities.

In conclusion, the classroom provides reliable resources and structure, whereas outdoor lessons offer direct observation. A planned combination makes use of both strengths and gives pupils opportunities that neither setting could provide alone.
